exercises.prompt: An empty wagon, `Wagon'(Empty_Mass => 22, Cargo => 0)`, is appended to the train. What is the last line the program prints?

feedback.message: Not yet: even an empty wagon has its own mass of 22 t.
Not yet: Wagon does not override Seats, so it inherits Vehicle's version, which returns 0.

hints: Which version of Seats does a Wagon use?
exercises.solution: The new wagon's `Mass` is 22 + 0 = 22, so the total becomes 258 + 22 = 280. `Wagon` inherits `Seats` from `Vehicle`, which returns 0, so the seats stay at 120: **Train: 280 t, 120 seats**.

exercises.prompt: `C` is declared as `C : Coach := …;` and `V` as a parameter of type `Vehicle'Class`. Which call dispatches at run time?

options.label: `V.Describe`
options.feedback: Yes. V is class-wide, so the tag of the actual object chooses which Describe runs.

options.label: `C.Describe`
options.feedback: Not yet: C has the specific type Coach, so the compiler binds the call to Coach's Describe statically.

options.label: Both
options.feedback: Not yet: in Ada only calls with a class-wide controlling argument dispatch.

hints: Which of the two has a class-wide type?
exercises.solution: Dispatching happens only when the controlling argument is class-wide. **`V.Describe`** dispatches; `C.Describe` is a statically bound call to `Coach`'s version. Being able to see this from the types is one of the reasons Ada OO suits analysable, real-time code.

feedback.message: Close: check the severity of an Overheat above 90 degrees, and the marker it earns.

hints: Log puts "!! " in front when the severity is at least 3.
exercises.solution: At 90 °C the severity is 2 (90 is not greater than 90), so the first line gets three spaces. At 91 °C it is 3, so the second line is **`!! minute 31: motor at 91 C`**.

exercises.prompt: In the valve program, the two calls in the main program are swapped, so `Fill_Tank (Fail => True);` comes first. How many times does `valve 1 opened` appear in the output now?

feedback.message: Not yet: where does the exception from the first call go, and does the second call ever run?

hints: The exception propagates out of Fill_Tank into Main.
Main's handler replaces the rest of Main's statements.
exercises.solution: The first call opens the valve, raises `Program_Error`, closes the valve during finalisation, and the exception propagates to `Main`, whose handler runs. The rest of `Main` (the second call) is abandoned, so `valve 1 opened` appears **1** time. The output is: valve 1 opened, filling..., valve 1 closed, handled the fault in Main.

exercises.prompt: Why do professional Ada programmers write `overriding` before every subprogram that overrides an inherited one?

options.label: So that a misspelt name or a wrong parameter type becomes a compile error instead of silently declaring a new, unrelated subprogram
options.feedback: Yes. The compiler checks that something is actually being overridden.

options.label: Because without it, the subprogram cannot dispatch
options.feedback: Not yet: overriding happens whether or not the indicator is written. The indicator only lets the compiler check your intent.

options.label: Because it makes the call faster
options.feedback: Not yet: it has no effect on the generated code.

hints: What did GNAT report when Describe was misspelt as Describ?
exercises.solution: The indicator states an intention that the compiler checks: `subprogram "Describ" is not overriding`. Without it, a typo creates a new primitive and the type silently keeps its parent's behaviour (or, as here, fails later with a less direct message). It costs nothing at run time.

exercises.prompt: A traffic-light controller has exactly three states, Red, Amber and Green, fixed by regulation. Each state has a different duration and a different next state. Which design fits Ada best?

options.label: An enumeration (or a discriminated record) handled with case statements
options.feedback: Yes. The set is closed, so case statements are simplest, and the compiler checks every state is handled.

options.label: An abstract tagged type State with three extensions and dispatching operations
options.feedback: Not yet: it would work, but it adds indirection and loses the compiler's completeness check for a set that never changes.

options.label: An interface implemented by three unrelated types
options.feedback: Not yet: interfaces suit capabilities shared by otherwise unrelated types, not three states of one machine.

hints: Is the set of kinds open or closed?
exercises.solution: A **closed** set of kinds is best modelled by an enumeration or a discriminated record with `case`: simpler code, no dispatching, and a compile error if a state is ever left unhandled. Tagged types pay off when the set of kinds is **open**, as with vehicles that may be added later by other teams.

exercises.prompt: Why does the train program use `Ada.Containers.Indefinite_Vectors` with `Element_Type => Vehicle'Class` rather than `Ada.Containers.Vectors`?

options.label: Values of Vehicle'Class can have different sizes (a Coach and a Wagon have different components), and only the indefinite containers hold elements whose size is not fixed
options.feedback: Yes. A class-wide type is indefinite, like String.

options.label: Ada.Containers.Vectors cannot hold records
options.feedback: Not yet: ordinary Vectors hold records happily, as long as every element has the same, fixed size.

options.label: Indefinite_Vectors is faster
options.feedback: Not yet: it is usually a little slower, since each element is allocated separately.

hints: Why did the word counter in Lesson 5 need Indefinite_Ordered_Maps for String keys?
exercises.solution: `Vehicle'Class` is an **indefinite** type: different specific types in the class have different sizes, so the container cannot reserve a fixed slot for each element. The `Indefinite_` containers allocate each element individually, which lets one vector hold locomotives, coaches and wagons together.
